analysis.one_liner: Establishes a government-funded single-payer national health program covering everyone, replacing Medicare, Medicaid, and employer insurance.
analysis.headline: The single-payer health care bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a national health insurance program run by the states under federal rules, covering every U.S. resident for a broad set of services — doctor and hospital care, prescription drugs, dental, vision, mental health, long-term care, and more — with no charge beyond limited cost-sharing for some services and none for low-income people. It would have replaced Medicare and Medicaid, banned private insurance that duplicates the public coverage, paid hospitals fixed annual budgets and doctors negotiated fee schedules, and paid for it with higher income and corporate taxes, higher tobacco and alcohol taxes, and payroll taxes. It never got past the committee referral stage.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain guaranteed coverage regardless of health condition, income, employment, age, or where they live, including dental, vision, mental health, substance abuse treatment, and long-term care that many current plans exclude. People with preexisting conditions, the uninsured, and families paying premiums and out-of-pocket costs would benefit most. Rural and medically underserved areas would get targeted subsidies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Grants every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident a right to comprehensive health services including primary and preventive care, hospital care, prescription drugs, dental, hearing, vision, mental health, substance abuse treatment, hospice, and long-term care, with automatic enrollment at birth [S3].

Prohibits states from limiting covered services based on preexisting conditions and bars discrimination in enrollment or service delivery based on health condition, income, age, race, sex, sexual preference, language, or residence in rural or urban areas [S3].

Bans private insurance that duplicates covered services and requires participating providers to accept the program payment as payment in full, eliminating premiums, deductibles, and balance billing for covered care [S3].

Replaces Medicare and Medicaid with the new program, extends coverage to all ages rather than only seniors and the poor, and adds benefits Medicare lacks, such as dental care, long-term care coordination, and prescription drug coverage under a nationally negotiated price list [S2] [S3].

Caps national health spending growth at the rate of growth of the gross national product, pays hospitals through negotiated global budgets, sets administrator-negotiated maximum prices for prescription drugs, and prohibits operating budgets from funding profit, marketing, or expansion — mechanisms aimed at holding down total health spending [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals would pay through higher income tax rates (15%, 28%, and 31% brackets rising to 20%, 31%, and 39%), new and higher payroll taxes on employees and employers, a new premium for people over 64, higher taxes on tobacco and alcohol, and the loss of the tax exclusion for employer-provided health coverage and the medical expense deduction. Corporations would pay a higher corporate rate (34% rising to 39%). Health insurers would lose the duplicative-coverage business, and providers would face fixed budgets and fee schedules.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises income tax rates on all brackets (top rate rising from 31% to 39%), raises the corporate rate from 34% to 39%, adds payroll taxes on employees and employers, and sharply increases tobacco and alcohol excise taxes — a large and immediate tax increase that its own text acknowledges, borne by working households as well as the wealthy [S3].

States must make their own matching contributions, and no individual is eligible for services unless their state puts up the required money — so residents of states that refuse or underfund could go uncovered despite the federal program [S2] [S3].

The plan bans private insurance duplicating covered services, eliminating the private health coverage most Americans then had and the choice it represented; providers must accept program rates as payment in full, and hospital operating budgets cannot fund profit, marketing, or new specialized equipment, which critics argued would constrain quality and innovation [S3].

A federal administrator would set the national health budget, approved drug lists, and maximum drug and equipment prices — concentrating vast pricing and coverage decisions in one federal office, a design critics considered an unwieldy expansion of federal power [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered universal coverage, the end of medical bankruptcy from uncovered care, and a single payment system with lower administrative costs, at the price of substantially higher taxes across income levels, the elimination of private employer-based insurance, and government-set budgets and prices for hospitals, doctors, and drugs. Those tradeoffs — universal coverage versus federal control of health spending — were the core of the 1993-94 health reform debate, and the bill never advanced far enough for Congress to weigh them in a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, referred to the Finance Committee, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Daniel Inouye introduced the National Health Care Act of 1993 on March 31, 1993, with Sen. Paul Wellstone as its sole cosponsor; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S1] [S4] [S5].
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor, dying when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

The bill was one of several single-payer proposals introduced in 1993 while the Clinton administration pursued its own competing employer-mandate health reform plan; none of the single-payer bills advanced [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the existing system remained: health insurers kept their market, employers kept the tax-favored group insurance system, and hospitals, physicians, and drug makers kept prevailing payment arrangements. The 103rd Congress ended in 1994 without enacting any national health program.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent health industries and the status quo

for.name: Sen. Daniel Inouye
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Health Care Act of 1993 and delivered introductory remarks.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: The Clinton administration
against.role: President and Health Care Task Force
against.what_they_did: Backed its own competing health reform plan (employer-mandate 'managed competition' approach) rather than single-payer legislation, absorbing the reform debate's momentum in 1993-94.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Ran public campaigns against government-run health insurance during the 1993-94 debate, including the widely seen 'Harry and Louise' advertising campaign.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only two Senate supporters, both Democrats, and died in committee without a vote, so no roll-call record shows how the parties would have divided.

industries.note: The bill bans sale of private insurance duplicating covered services and repeals employer-based coverage, eliminating insurers' core business. Insurers' interest ran against the bill's universal-coverage guarantee.

Hospitals would be paid through negotiated global annual budgets with no profit, marketing, or unapproved equipment spending, ending cost-based charges and uncompensated-care burdens but capping revenue and expansion.

Doctors would get guaranteed payment under negotiated fee schedules and an end to insurance paperwork, but must accept program rates as payment in full and face spending targets if they exceed annual targets.
A federal administrator would set maximum prices for prescription drugs and could exclude 'overpriced' drugs when better alternatives exist, replacing the current largely unregulated pricing market.
The bill sharply raises excise taxes on cigarettes, distilled spirits, wine, and beer and imposes one-time floor-stocks taxes, costs the industries would pass to consumers.
Employers would face new payroll taxes and a levy tied to retiree health coverage, but would shed the obligation and tax treatment of providing employee health insurance.
Top income tax rates rise from 31% to 39%, estate and minimum tax rates increase, and more Social Security benefits become taxable — progressive taxes funding the program.
